title: UROFACIAL SYNDROME 1
alt_titles: FACIAL PALSY, PARTIAL, WITH URINARY ABNORMALITIES
INVERTED SMILE AND OCCULT NEUROPATHIC BLADDER

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene (613469) on chromosome 10q24.2.

checks.claim: Urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene for UFS.

checks.claim: The HPSE2 gene is located on chromosome 10q24.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Previously, we localized the defective gene for the urofacial syndrome (UFS) to a region on chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping.
checks.explanation: The abstract gives the region as 10q24. The more precise band 10q24.2 is standard gene-location nomenclature, so it counts as supported.

paragraphs.text: Urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Its cardinal features are an abnormal, 'inverted' facial expression, in which patients appear to cry when they try to smile, and congenital obstructive uropathy (Wang et al., 1997; Derbent et al., 2009). The bladder fails to empty completely even though there is no anatomic outflow obstruction or overt neurologic damage. The resulting neurogenic bladder with voiding dysfunction leads to enuresis, urinary tract infection and hydronephrosis (Wang et al., 1997; Daly et al., 2010). Affected individuals often have reflux of infected urine to the upper renal tract, which puts the kidneys at risk of damage and renal failure (Daly et al., 2010). Some severely affected patients become hypertensive and progress to end-stage renal disease (Derbent et al., 2009).

paragraphs.text: Elejalde (1979) described 7 patients (4 females and 3 males) from 3 unrelated families, one of them consanguineous (first cousins). The patients had peculiar facies and gestures when smiling and crying. Their urinary findings included hydronephrosis, hydroureter and intravesical stenosis of the ureter. Other findings were an abnormal caliber of the urethra in its prostatic and membranous portions, urethral valves, and an abnormal bladder with trabeculation and diverticula, associated with severe hypertrophy of the mucosa with sclerotic changes.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1997) performed a genome screen combining homozygosity mapping and DNA pooling in 20 patients with urofacial syndrome. Marker D10S677 was linked to and associated with the disorder, with excess homozygosity in patients (P less than 10(-6)). On haplotype analysis, all 31 patients were homozygous for D10S1726 and D10S198, which lie about 5 cM telomeric to D10S677, compared with 12% of unaffected relatives (P less than 10(-19)). Recombinations placed the gene within a 1-cM interval between D10S1433 and D10S603 on chromosome 10q23-q24.
